text: And we are seeing almost daily this re-escalation of the war there. Interesting that this meeting is going in place as that happens. Joining me now is former White House Chief of Staff Mick Mulvaney. Mick, what do you think about this latest escalation? It seems like this is going to be the rhythm of things for quite some time. Yeah, you know, I've talked about this, Laura,
that I think this war will continue on in one way, shape or form for quite a long time. And the reason is the motivation behind what I think we just saw here

in the last couple of hours or minutes, which is I think Iran wants the war. I think we're slowly coming to the realization in this country, and certainly they are in the Trump administration, that the current regime in Iran is happy with the war going on.
Why does that?
It probably allows them to simply reinforce their control over their own country.

They're not interested right now in ending it. They're interested in dragging it out as long as they possibly can. And plus, they believe for a variety of reasons that time is on their side, whether or not that's political with the midterms, which I think is wrong. It's economic, which is possible.
Donald Trump himself suggested that one of the reasons he signed the original ceasefire

was because of the economic impact. And number three, and this is the most concerning, is that there were leaks out of the Trump administration that perhaps the American military is running out of weapons. That is a significant problem, by the way. That leak would cause me a great deal of consternation as the chief of staff. But in any event, for one or more of those reasons, perhaps Iran thinks that if they can drag this out, the better result for them.

And that is a formula for things not wrapping up anytime soon. We've talked about the tension between Trump and Netanyahu before. He's at the White House right now. The two have met. Very unusual for Trump to agree to or say that there are no cameras. There's only still shots from that meeting. But given that we know from reporting that it was Netanyahu who had a big part in convincing Trump to enter this war, and he convinced him that it wouldn't be a forever war and it would be, you know, a fairly quick timeline, what do you think these conversations are like now?
Would Donald Trump be holding that to Netanyahu, reminding him that perhaps he was wrong?
A couple of things.
Keep in mind that Trump would never make the decision based upon that information from one person. If Netanyahu did say that,
I don't have any classified information, so I can't give anything away here.

But if Netanyahu did say that, I highly, highly doubt that Trump would make a decision based upon that simple confirmation or conversation, which is to say that somebody else that he listens to probably had to tell him something similar. Trump doesn't listen to any one person. He listens to a universe of people.
Could Lindsey Graham have been encouraging him
to begin the war?
Yes, he probably could have.
Is that voice gone? Yes, it is.
So that could certainly change the balance.
But I think it's wrong to think, and look, I get this question a lot all the way around the world,
did Netanyahu drag Trump into this war?
I just don't see it like that.
But if your question is,
is Trump going to point out to Netanyahu in this meeting
that you told me this was going to be easier than it is? Absolutely.
That's how Donald Trump works. That's how he uses the leverage in the conversations and so forth. So, yeah.
No, I think Netanyahu could probably expect a stern talking to,
but I don't think you read into that, Laura, that the relationship is frayed in any way. Let's not lose track of the fact

they're meeting at the Oval Office. If Donald Trump was really that upset with Netanyahu, this meeting wouldn't even be taking place. Yeah, true. So, no, I think the relationship is solid. But, yeah, Netanyahu's good to hear a little bit from Trump about how they got where they are right now.

You mentioned Lindsey Graham's influence on Trump that he's, of course, no longer. His funeral was held today. This is what Donald Trump had to say about Lindsey Graham. A giant of the United States Senate and a true American original who left us much too soon.
And that can only be the one and only Lindsey Graham. He was extremely hawkish. I will tell you, he never saw a war that he didn't like. He never saw a war that he didn't like.
Is that what you know of Lindsey Graham too?
Yep, absolutely. In fact, it's not lost on me, Laura,

that that was actually printed in the script. Most of the speech today was off the script, so that wasn't Trump freewheeling. That actually got approved by somebody, and rightly so. Look, Lindsey was an interventionist. He was a neoconservative. I was not. And, again, he was my senator. I mean, I've known Lindsey for 20 years. I'm sitting tonight in South Carolina, where Lindsey was from, so we were close. But he liked war.
There's no question about it. Excuse me. I should say... Let's say it this way.
He appreciated the ability
to continue American foreign policy
through kinetic action. That's how he would put it.
Kinetic action.
Yeah, that's exactly right.
What are you familiar with?
Trump is not wrong.
That voice is gone now
in the Republican Party in Washington, D.C.
Why did he? Did he like these fervor wars? Did he not care about what they did
to America's, I guess, perception at home and abroad and the cost of it?
Lindsey believed very firmly in peace through strength.
I do too. He also believed that occasionally you had to prove that strength to people and that sometimes war was the only... ..was diplomacy taken to the next level.
And there are certain people around the world who only understand strength. By the way, I happen to agree with that philosophically.
The Iranians understand strength much more so than they do, say, negotiation and diplomacy. And they're not the only ones.
Lindsey was not shy about using American military strength to further American interests.
